chapterNote.lost: What varies is the texture. The Hebrew keeps a verb for creating, the hovering Spirit and the feasts behind the lights. The Greek keeps a firm firmament, an extra approval on day two, a fuller account of the waters and the wording the New Testament quotes. The Latin and King James mostly follow the Hebrew shape, each with small turns of its own.

study-earth.name: Earth / land
study-earth.text: The wording can refer to earth, dry land or ground according to the sentence. In Genesis 1 the dry land receives a name and brings forth vegetation. Use the occurrences below to follow this chapter’s particular setting.

study-heaven.name: Heaven / sky
study-heaven.text: Follow the local use of heaven or sky. In Genesis 1 the firmament is named Heaven and the lights are placed in relation to it. A mention here should not automatically be read as a description of the later theological idea of heaven.

god-theos.name: God (Theos)
god-theos.text: Entry focus: Red. This entry studies a name or designation of God in the Father/Creator section. Shared titles are not restricted to the Father in every passage. title or designation yet to us there is one God, the Father, of whom are all things, and we for him; and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things, and we live through him. The Greek word theos is translated “God” or “god” according to its context. Paul confesses one God, the Father, while also confessing one Lord, Jesus Christ. John calls the Word God and records Thomas addressing the risen Jesus as “my God.” These texts inform Christian teaching about divine identity; the vocabulary itself is not a list of separate deities. Scope: Placed under Father for navigation. This designation concerns God and is not, on lexical grounds alone, restricted to the Father in Christian theology. term-pneuma-ruach.name: Pneuma / Ruach
term-pneuma-ruach.text: Greek: πνεῦμα (pneuma) · Hebrew: רוּחַ Greek pneuma and Hebrew ruach can refer to wind, breath, or spirit, depending on context. John 3:8 draws on the relationship between wind and Spirit; Ezekiel 37 moves through imagery of breath, winds, and God’s spirit. These overlapping meanings enrich the passages without making every occurrence a reference to the Holy Spirit. Read the sources: John 3:8 (World English Bible) · Ezekiel 37:1–14, Hebrew and English (Mechon Mamre) · Mounce: Greek headword

spirit-god-lord.name: Spirit of God
spirit-god-lord.text: Entry focus: Violet. This entry studies a designation associated with the Holy Spirit; its stated contextual and interpretive qualifications remain in force. title or designation The earth was formless and empty. Darkness was on the surface of the deep and God’s Spirit was hovering over the surface of the waters. Scripture speaks of God’s Spirit in creation, empowerment, and divine presence. Genesis 1:2 is rendered “God’s Spirit” in the WEB; the Hebrew term can also denote wind or breath, and translations of this verse differ. Isaiah describes Yahweh’s Spirit resting on the promised ruler with wisdom, understanding, counsel, might, knowledge, and reverence. Christian readers relate these passages to the Holy Spirit. Scope: This entry concerns a designation or interpretation associated with the Holy Spirit; it does not identify an additional divine being. Hebrew: רוּחַ אֱלֹהִים · ruaḥ elohim Original-language source — Phrase shown without cantillation marks and the preceding conjunction. Greek: Πνεῦμα Θεοῦ · pneuma theou Original-language source Biblical context: Genesis 1:1–3; Isaiah 11:1–5; Romans 8:9–16 Historical and interpretive sources: NET Bible translators’ note on Genesis 1:2 — Explains Spirit of God, wind from God, and mighty wind as interpretive translation options. Related forms: Spirit of the Lord; Spirit of Yahweh; Spirit of wisdom and understanding; Spirit of counsel and might; Spirit of knowledge and fear of Yahweh Shared relationship: Spirit of God / Spirit of your Father: Father-category cross-reference. This relates the Spirit to the Father; it does not identify the Father and the Holy Spirit as the same person. Paraclete: two complementary study emphases. Paraclete represents the Greek παράκλητος (paraklētos). English Bibles render it Advocate, Counselor, Helper, or Comforter. The following entries distinguish legal and judicial emphasis from guidance, support, and consolation. These senses overlap. “Counselor” can itself carry a legal sense; this arrangement is an editorial distinction, not a separation into different Greek names. study-firmament.name: Firmament
study-firmament.text: In Genesis 1 the firmament separates the waters and is named Heaven. Read its stated location and function before assigning a modern physical model. Compare the chapter translation notes and the matched verses.

readings.saints: In the beginning God made heaven and earth.
readings.hebrew: In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth.
readings.latin: In the beginning God created heaven and earth.
readings.kjv: In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth.

verses.received: In the beginning, God made heaven and earth.
verses.explain: The Bible opens with God, not with the world. Before any light, land or living thing appears, one actor is named, and everything that exists is traced back to him. Heaven and earth together stand for the whole of creation, so nothing in the account that follows falls outside his work.
shared: God is the one who acts.
Heaven and earth are his work.

instructions.text: God made heaven and earth, and the world had a beginning.
Begin with God when asking where things come from and what they are for.

lost.text: Hebrew bara becomes the everyday ἐποίησεν, “made.” The Greek still says God did it, but a verb the Bible uses only with God as subject is gone. Latin creavit and King James “created” keep a separate word for creating.
ἐν ἀρχῇ is the exact opening of John 1:1. The Latin and King James keep that echo through their own New Testaments, with in principio and “In the beginning.”
The plural form of Hebrew shamayim becomes singular in the Greek, Latin and King James. The site’s note treats this as a natural rendering, not a change of meaning.

verses.siteNote: Hebrew bereshit bara Elohim uses bara, “created.” In this creative sense and verb form (Qal), the verb denotes divine activity; that statement should not be extended to every Hebrew form spelled with the same consonants. Greek en archē epoiēsen ho theos uses poieō, “make,” which also renders Hebrew asah elsewhere in this chapter. This reduces a lexical distinction without denying divine creation. Hebrew shamayim is plural in form; Greek ouranos is singular. The opening en archē recurs in John 1:1. Lexical reference: Brown–Driver–Briggs, ברא I, Qal.
verses.whyNote: Translation-based hypothesis. The correspondence of bara with poieō in 1:1, 1:21 and 1:27 supports a recurring translation choice. Singular “heaven” can naturally represent the Hebrew plural-form noun. Neither observation requires a different Hebrew source. The temporal-versus-independent interpretation of the opening concerns syntax; these readings alone do not establish a manuscript variant.

words.note: John opens his Gospel with the same two Greek words, so the story of the Word starts where creation starts.
The Greek uses the ordinary word for making. The Hebrew bara' is a verb the Bible uses only with God as its subject.

readings.saints: But the earth was unseen and unformed, and darkness was over the abyss; and the Spirit of God was being carried over the water.
readings.hebrew: The earth was waste and empty, and darkness was over the face of the deep; and the Spirit of God was hovering over the face of the waters.
readings.latin: The earth was empty and vacant, and darkness lay over the face of the deep, and the Spirit of God moved over the waters.
readings.kjv: And the earth was without form, and void; and darkness was upon the face of the deep. And the Spirit of God moved upon the face of the waters.

verses.received: Before God ordered it, the earth was dark, unfinished and under water, and the Spirit of God was present over it.
verses.explain: Each translation describes the earth as not yet ready: lacking form, fullness or order. The scene is dark and covered by the deep. Yet it is not abandoned, because the Spirit of God is already there over the waters before the first command is spoken.
shared: The earth was not yet ordered or filled.
The Spirit of God was over the waters.

instructions.text: The Spirit of God was present over the earth before it was ordered.
Emptiness and darkness are not beyond God's presence.

lost.text: ἀόρατος καὶ ἀκατασκεύαστος pictures an earth not yet seen and not yet fitted out. This sense of hidden and unready belongs to the Greek alone.

Hebrew tohu va-vohu is a rhyming pair of waste and emptiness that returns in Jeremiah 4:23 when the land is undone. The Greek drops both the sound and the echo. Latin inanis et vacua and King James “without form, and void” stay nearer the idea of emptiness.
The Hebrew Spirit is “hovering,” a close and watchful image. Greek ἐπεφέρετο, “was being carried,” gives movement instead. Latin ferebatur follows the Greek, and King James “moved” is plainer still.
πνεῦμα and Hebrew ruach can both mean spirit, breath or wind, so a capital S in English is already an interpretation.

verses.siteNote: Hebrew תֹהוּ וָבֹהוּ (tohu va-vohu) describes waste and emptiness; Greek ἀόρατος καὶ ἀκατασκεύαστος describes what is unseen and unformed. Hebrew meraḥefet presents hovering, while Greek epephereto presents movement over the water. The project’s two English columns preserve these different images. Both Hebrew ruach and Greek pneuma can mean spirit or wind. Neither the capitalization of “Spirit” nor the English word “unformed” alone settles the passage’s later theological interpretation.
verses.whyNote: Proposed explanation; origin unresolved. A plausible explanation is contextual translation: the Greek describes the earth through visibility and readiness for ordering, while the Hebrew idiom emphasizes desolation and emptiness. The movement verb likewise offers a Greek way of expressing activity over water. These are working inferences from the wording, not a recovered statement of the translator’s intentions. A philosophical background might be investigated, but these words alone do not establish dependence on a particular school. Later rabbinic or Trinitarian readings explain reception, not necessarily the origin of the difference.

words.greek: aoratos kai akataskeuastos (ἀόρατος καὶ ἀκατασκεύαστος); Hebrew tohu wa-bohu
words.note: The Greek describes an earth not yet seen and not yet fitted out. The Hebrew uses a rhyming pair, tohu wa-bohu, that returns when Jeremiah sees the land undone.

words.greek: pneuma theou (πνεῦμα θεοῦ); Hebrew ruach elohim
words.note: Both pneuma and ruach mean breath, wind and spirit. Christian readers from the earliest centuries saw here the first appearance of the Holy Spirit.

readings.saints: God said, “Let light come into being,” and light came into being.
readings.hebrew: God said, “Let there be light,” and there was light.
readings.latin: God said, “Let there be light.” And there was light.
readings.kjv: And God said, Let there be light: and there was light.

verses.received: God speaks, and light exists.
verses.explain: This is the first time God speaks in the Bible, and his word is enough. There is no struggle, tool or delay between the command and the result. What God says happens, and that pattern shapes the rest of the chapter.
shared: Light came exactly as he said.

instructions.text: God's word brings about what he says.
Take God's word seriously, because it is effective.

lost.text: Γενηθήτω and ἐγένετο stress something coming into being. English “let there be” can sound more like simple existence.
All four keep the word-for-word echo between command and result, so the message itself does not change.

verses.siteNote: Hebrew yehi or va-yehi or pairs a command form and a narrative form of the same verb hayah, “to be,” so command and fulfillment echo word for word. Greek genēthētō phōs kai egeneto phōs reproduces that echo with ginomai, “to come into being,” a verb that slightly stresses coming-to-be rather than simple existence.
verses.whyNote: Translation-based observation. The Greek translator followed the Hebrew word order and repetition closely here, choosing ginomai as the standard equivalent of hayah in the creation formula. Because the Greek preserves the echo, Jewish and Christian readers worked from effectively the same sentence; their different emphases arise in interpretation, not in the text.

words.note: Creation happens by God speaking, again and again through the chapter. The Psalms and Hebrews take this up: the heavens were made by His word.
Light comes on the first day, before the sun on the fourth. Paul says the God who called light out of darkness has shone in our hearts.

readings.saints: God saw that the light was good, and God separated the light from the darkness.
readings.hebrew: God saw that the light was good, and God separated the light from the darkness.
readings.latin: God saw that the light was good, and He separated the light from the darkness.
readings.kjv: And God saw the light, that it was good: and God divided the light from the darkness.

verses.received: God sees that the light is good and separates it from the darkness.
verses.explain: God does more than make the light. He looks at it, judges it good and gives it a distinct place apart from the darkness. Creation here is shown as deliberate and ordered, with God as the one who decides what is good.

instructions.text: God judges what is good, and he separated light from darkness.
Let God's judgment set the standard for what you call good.

lost.text: καλόν means both good and beautiful, so God’s verdict covers worth and loveliness together. Hebrew tov, Latin bona and English “good” do not carry “beautiful” in the same way on the surface.

verses.siteNote: Hebrew ki tov, “that it was good,” becomes Greek hoti kalon, a word that joins goodness with fittingness and beauty. Hebrew va-yavdel … bein … u-vein, “separated between … and between,” is mirrored by Greek diechōrisen … ana meson … kai ana meson, a Hebrew idiom carried straight into Greek.
verses.whyNote: Comparison-based observation. The Greek repeats the “between … and between” construction of the Hebrew. In this verse, that close correspondence preserves both God’s evaluation of the light and His act of separation. No additional event or contrary judgment appears in either reading.

words.note: Greek kalos means both good and beautiful, so the verdict covers worth and loveliness together. It returns at the end of each day's work.

readings.saints: God called the light Day, and the darkness He called Night. There was evening and there was morning: day one.
readings.hebrew: God called the light Day, and the darkness He called Night. There was evening and there was morning: day one.
readings.latin: God called the light Day, and the darkness Night. Evening came, and morning came: one day.
readings.kjv: And God called the light Day, and the darkness he called Night. And the evening and the morning were the first day.

verses.received: God names the light and the darkness, and evening and morning complete the first day of the account.
verses.explain: Light becomes Day and darkness becomes Night because God names them. Giving a name shows his authority over what he has made. Evening and morning then close the day, beginning the rhythm that orders the whole chapter.
shared: Evening and morning closed the day.

instructions.text: God named day and night, and time has an order given by him.
Receive each day as part of an order God established.

lost.text: ἡμέρα μία says “one day,” not “first day.” Hebrew yom echad and Latin dies unus agree. Only the King James smooths it to “the first day,” hiding an oddity the Greek preserved for readers such as Basil.
Greek and Hebrew repeat “there was” for evening and for morning. The Latin uses the verb once, and the King James compresses the refrain to “the evening and the morning were.”

verses.siteNote: Hebrew yom echad uses the cardinal “one,” although days two to six use ordinals (“second,” “third”). Greek hēmera mia keeps the cardinal instead of smoothing it to prōtē, “first.” Both also place evening before morning in the closing refrain.
verses.whyNote: Translation-based observation. The translator preserved an irregular Hebrew expression rather than normalizing it to the ordinal pattern of the other days. That choice kept the feature available to Greek-reading Christians, which is why Basil could comment on the same anomaly that the rabbis discussed in Hebrew.

words.note: In the ancient world, naming showed authority. God names day, night, heaven, earth and seas; later He hands this work of naming to Adam.

readings.saints: God said, “Let there be a firmament in the midst of the water, and let it separate water from water.” And it was so.
readings.hebrew: God said, “Let there be an expanse in the midst of the waters, and let it separate water from water.”
readings.latin: God also said, “Let there be a firmament in the midst of the waters, and let it separate waters from waters.”
readings.kjv: And God said, Let there be a firmament in the midst of the waters, and let it divide the waters from the waters.

verses.received: God commands a firmament in the midst of the waters to separate water from water.
verses.explain: The second day begins as the first did, with God speaking. His command makes room within the waters by dividing them. Order is again brought about by his word and by separation, preparing a place for what comes later.
shared: He commanded something in the midst of the waters.
Its purpose was to separate water from water.

instructions.text: God commanded order within the waters by his word.

lost.text: στερέωμα means something made firm. Latin firmamentum and King James “firmament” carry that Greek idea into the Western Bible.
Hebrew raqia comes from a verb for hammering or spreading out thin. The Greek firmness replaces that image of something beaten out, and the Latin and King James inherit the replacement.
Only the Greek says “and it was so” here, directly after the command. The Hebrew, Latin and King James wait until 1:7.

verses.siteNote: Hebrew raqia, here “expanse,” is related to spreading or beating out; Greek stereōma, “firmament,” emphasizes firmness. The English contrast must not imply that the Hebrew word necessarily describes an immaterial or purely empty space. Brown–Driver–Briggs, רקיע discusses the ancient conception of the sky. Greek also places kai egeneto houtōs, “and it was so,” after the command here; Hebrew places the corresponding formula at the end of 1:7.
verses.whyNote: Pattern-supported hypothesis. The position of “and it was so” makes the Greek command and fulfillment formula agree with several nearby passages (1:9, 11, 15, 20, 24, 30). This is a pattern observed in the cited texts, not proof of the translator’s intention or of an earlier Hebrew reading. The lexical correspondence raqia/stereōma does not by itself establish the adoption of an entire Greek cosmological system.

words.note: Greek stereōma means something made firm; Latin firmamentum carries the idea into English. The Hebrew raqia' comes from a verb for hammering metal out thin.

readings.saints: God made the firmament, and God separated the water below the firmament from the water above the firmament.
readings.hebrew: God made the expanse and separated the waters below the expanse from the waters above the expanse. And it was so.
readings.latin: God made the firmament and separated the waters beneath the firmament from those above the firmament. And so it was.
readings.kjv: And God made the firmament, and divided the waters which were under the firmament from the waters which were above the firmament: and it was so.

verses.received: God makes the firmament and separates the waters below it from the waters above it.
verses.explain: The command of the previous verse is now carried out. God himself makes what he spoke of, and the waters are divided into those below and those above. The verse shows his word and his work matching exactly.

instructions.text: God does what he says he will do.
God's actions can be trusted to match his words.

lost.text: “And it was so” is absent from the Greek here because it already appeared in 1:6. Read together, both verses tell the same event in a different order.
The Greek names God again as the one who separates. The Hebrew, Latin and King James let one subject carry both actions.

verses.siteNote: The Hebrew closes the act with va-yehi khen, “and it was so”; the Greek has already used that formula in 1:6 and omits it here. The Greek also repeats ho theos as the subject of separating, where the Hebrew lets one subject govern both verbs. Hebrew mayim is plural in form; Greek uses singular hydōr, “water.”
verses.whyNote: Pattern-supported hypothesis. Read with 1:6, the formula occupies a different position rather than simply disappearing from the creation sequence. Repeating “God” also makes the subject explicit. Such changes can arise in translation or textual transmission; this comparison establishes their presence, not their historical origin.

words.greek: to hydōr to epanō tou stereōmatos (τὸ ὕδωρ τὸ ἐπάνω τοῦ στερεώματος)
words.note: The waters above are called to praise God alongside sun, moon and stars in the Psalms.

readings.saints: God called the firmament Heaven. And God saw that it was good. There was evening and there was morning: a second day.
readings.hebrew: God called the expanse Heavens. There was evening and there was morning: a second day.
readings.latin: God called the firmament Heaven. Evening came, and morning came: the second day.
readings.kjv: And God called the firmament Heaven. And the evening and the morning were the second day.

verses.received: God names the firmament Heaven, and the second day ends.
verses.explain: As with Day and Night, God gives what he has made its name. The sky above is not a rival power or a god in its own right. It is something God made and named, and with it the second day closes.

instructions.text: The sky is something God made and named.
Honor the maker of the heavens, not the heavens themselves.

lost.text: Only the Greek says “God saw that it was good” here, so every day of making receives God’s approval.
In the Hebrew, Latin and King James, the second day alone has no approval. A reader of the Greek cannot notice that silence.

verses.siteNote: The Greek contains kai eiden ho theos hoti kalon, “and God saw that it was good,” which the Hebrew of this verse lacks; in the Hebrew the second day is the only day of the six without that approval. Hebrew shamayim (plural in form) again becomes singular ouranos.
verses.whyNote: Origin unresolved. The longer Greek reading gives day two an approval like the other days, so alignment with a repeated formula is a plausible explanation. These two editions alone cannot determine whether the difference arose in Greek translation or in the Hebrew transmission behind the readings. Rashi interprets the shorter form as meaningful; his reception is not manuscript evidence for how it originated.

words.note: The Hebrew word is plural in form; the Greek here is singular. The New Testament often keeps the plural, as in "Our Father who art in the heavens".

words.greek: eiden ho theos hoti kalon (εἶδεν ὁ θεὸς ὅτι καλόν)
words.note: The Hebrew text has no word of approval on the second day. The Greek includes it, so every day of making ends with God seeing that it is good.

readings.saints: God said, “Let the water below heaven be gathered into one gathering, and let the dry land appear.” And it was so. The water below heaven was gathered into its gatherings, and the dry land appeared.
readings.hebrew: God said, “Let the waters below the heavens be gathered into one place, and let the dry land appear.” And it was so.
readings.latin: God said, “Let the waters beneath heaven gather into one place, and let dry land appear.” And so it was.
readings.kjv: And God said, Let the waters under the heaven be gathered together unto one place, and let the dry land appear: and it was so.

verses.received: God gathers the waters below heaven so that dry land appears.
verses.explain: The waters that covered everything now move at God's word, and dry land comes into view. The sea has no power to resist him. A place is being prepared where plants, animals and people will live.
shared: God commanded the waters to be gathered.
He commanded dry land to appear.

instructions.text: The waters and the dry land took their places at God's command.
The powers of nature stay under God's authority.

lost.text: Only the Greek adds a full fulfilment: the water was gathered into its gatherings and the dry land appeared. The Hebrew, Latin and King James end at “it was so.”
συναγωγή is the word behind “synagogue,” a gathering. The Hebrew, Latin and King James say “one place,” so that picture of assembling is lost.
The Greek moves from “one gathering” in the command to plural “gatherings” in the fulfilment, a shift the shorter witnesses never show.

verses.siteNote: Hebrew el maqom echad, “into one place,” corresponds to Greek eis synagōgēn mian, “into one gathering.” Both have “and it was so.” Greek then supplies a further narrated fulfillment: the water is gathered eis tas synagōgas autōn, “into its/their gatherings,” and the dry land appears. Hebrew lacks this additional sentence, not every statement of fulfillment. The Greek possessive is plural even though hydōr, “water,” is grammatically singular.
verses.whyNote: Origin unresolved. Greek “gathering” may express the collecting action already present in the command. Its relationship to Hebrew miqveh, “gathering,” in 1:10 is also worth comparing, but reconstructing that noun in a lost Hebrew source would be a hypothesis. The extra fulfillment sentence fits the surrounding command-and-deed pattern. Neither observation identifies an attested manuscript change or proves its direction.

words.note: The Greek word is synagogue, a gathering. The Hebrew says the waters gather into one place.
This closing sentence, telling how the command was carried out, is in the Greek but not in the Hebrew text.

readings.saints: God called the dry land Earth, and the gatherings of the waters He called Seas. God saw that it was good.
readings.hebrew: God called the dry land Earth, and the gathering of the waters He called Seas. God saw that it was good.
readings.latin: God called the dry land Earth, and the gatherings of water He called Seas. God saw that it was good.
readings.kjv: And God called the dry land Earth; and the gathering together of the waters called he Seas: and God saw that it was good.

verses.received: God names the dry land Earth and the waters Seas, and sees that it is good.
verses.explain: God names both land and sea, showing that each belongs to him. He then looks at what he has done and declares it good. The world taking shape is approved by the one who made it.
shared: God called the dry land Earth.
He called the gathered waters Seas.
God saw that it was good.

instructions.text: God called the land and the seas good.
Treat the land and the sea as good gifts of God.

lost.text: Greek συστέματα and Latin congregationes are plural, “gatherings.” Hebrew miqveh and King James “gathering together” are singular. All four still name them Seas.
The Greek changes noun from συναγωγή in 1:9 to συστέματα here, so the link between the two verses is looser than in the Hebrew, Latin or King James words for gathering.

verses.siteNote: Hebrew miqveh ha-mayim, “the gathering of the waters,” is a collective singular; Greek ta systēmata tōn hydatōn makes it plural, “the gatherings.” Both then name them yammim / thalassai, “Seas,” in the plural, and both give the approval ki tov / hoti kalon.
verses.whyNote: Translation-based hypothesis. Greek plural “gatherings” fits its plural wording in 1:9 and the plural “Seas.” Adjustment of grammatical number is a plausible explanation, but “Seas” does not grammatically require the preceding noun to be plural. These readings alone do not exclude a difference in the translator’s Hebrew source.

words.note: God sets the seas in their bounds. In John's vision of the new creation, the sea is no more.

readings.saints: God said, “Let the earth sprout vegetation: plants sowing seed according to kind and likeness, and fruit trees bearing fruit, with their seed in them according to kind, upon the earth.” And it was so.
readings.hebrew: God said, “Let the earth sprout vegetation: plants yielding seed, and fruit trees bearing fruit according to their kind, with their seed in them, upon the earth.” And it was so.
readings.latin: He said, “Let the earth bring forth green plants bearing seed, and fruit trees bearing fruit according to their kind, with their seed within them upon the earth.” And so it was.
readings.kjv: And God said, Let the earth bring forth grass, the herb yielding seed, and the fruit tree yielding fruit after his kind, whose seed is in itself, upon the earth: and it was so.

verses.received: God commands the earth to produce plants and fruit trees that carry their own seed.
verses.explain: Life first appears here, again at God's word. The earth is told to bring it forth, and the plants carry seed within them, so life can continue from one generation to the next. God is providing for a world that will go on.
shared: Plants and fruit trees were commanded.
They carry seed for new life.

instructions.text: Plants and trees carry seed because God made them to continue.
The growth of food and fruit depends on God's design.

lost.text: Only the Greek says “according to kind and likeness.” Its word for likeness is close to the one used of humanity in 1:26, a connection the other three do not show.
The Greek applies “according to kind” to the plants in the command. The Hebrew, Latin and King James apply it here only to the fruit tree.

flags: Swete’s text also has εἰς ὁμοιότητα after the tree’s “according to kind.” Saints English does not translate it, so the two Greek texts need comparing here.
verses.siteNote: Hebrew esev mazria zera, “plants yielding seed,” carries no kind-formula; only the fruit tree is le-mino, “according to its kind.” Greek chortou speiron sperma kata genos kai kath’ homoiotēta gives the plants both “kind” and “likeness” (homoiotēs). The Hebrew also calls the tree ets peri oseh peri, literally “a fruit-tree making fruit.”
verses.whyNote: Pattern-supported hypothesis. Greek applies the kind-formula to the plants in the command as well as its fulfillment, while Hebrew first applies it to the plants in 1:12. Greek also has “and likeness” in both verses. These correspondences support a suggestion of fuller alignment between command and fulfillment; they do not establish when or by whom the wording developed. The Greek word homoiotēs here is related to, but is not the same noun as, homoiōsis in 1:26.

words.note: The first seed in Scripture is a plant's. The same word then carries the promise of offspring, from the woman's seed to Abraham's.

words.greek: kata genos kai kath' homoiotēta (κατὰ γένος καὶ καθ' ὁμοιότητα)
words.note: The Hebrew says only "according to its kind". The Greek adds likeness, a word close to the one used of man in 1:26.

readings.saints: The earth brought forth vegetation: plants sowing seed according to kind and likeness, and fruit trees bearing fruit, with their seed in them according to kind, upon the earth. God saw that it was good.
readings.hebrew: The earth brought forth vegetation: plants yielding seed according to their kind, and trees bearing fruit with their seed in them according to their kind. God saw that it was good.
readings.latin: The earth brought forth green plants bearing seed according to their kind, and trees bearing fruit, each having seed according to its kind. God saw that it was good.
readings.kjv: And the earth brought forth grass, and herb yielding seed after his kind, and the tree yielding fruit, whose seed was in itself, after his kind: and God saw that it was good.

verses.received: The earth obeys, producing the plants and trees God commanded, and God sees that it is good.
verses.explain: What God commanded in the previous verse now happens. The earth brings forth plants and fruit-bearing trees, each according to its kind, with seed for the future. God looks at this living growth and calls it good.
shared: It brought forth trees bearing fruit.
God saw that it was good.

instructions.text: The earth produced what God commanded, and he saw that it was good.
Fruitfulness comes from responding to what God has spoken.

lost.text: The Greek repeats the description from 1:11, so the fulfilment mirrors the command closely.
The Hebrew shifts from “a fruit-tree making fruit” in the command to “a tree making fruit” here. The Greek’s repetition hides that small change.

verses.siteNote: Hebrew now applies “according to its kind” to the plants and has ets oseh peri, “a tree making fruit,” rather than the command’s ets peri oseh peri, “a fruit-tree making fruit.” Greek repeats the botanical description from 1:11, including xylon karpimon, “fruitful tree,” “and likeness,” and “upon the earth.” The entire verses are not identical: the command becomes a narrated action, followed here by approval.
verses.whyNote: Pattern-supported hypothesis. The repeated Greek botanical description aligns command and fulfillment more closely than the Hebrew wording does. Alignment is an inference from this pair of verses, not a rule without exceptions throughout the chapter. Rashi shows how the Hebrew differences were interpreted; his commentary cannot settle which textual form developed first.

readings.saints: There was evening and there was morning: a third day.
readings.hebrew: There was evening and there was morning: a third day.
readings.latin: Evening came, and morning came: the third day.
readings.kjv: And the evening and the morning were the third day.

verses.received: Evening and morning complete the third day.
verses.explain: The steady refrain returns. Land, sea and growing things are now in place, and the day closes just as the others have. The repetition reassures the reader that creation is moving forward in the order God has set.

instructions.text: God's work moves forward in an ordered sequence of days.

lost.text: Nothing here changes the message. The Latin and King James compress the refrain just as they do in 1:5.

verses.siteNote: The refrain closes the third day, whose two approvals occur in 1:10 and 1:12. The sixth day also has two evaluations, at 1:25 and 1:31, the latter calling the whole creation “very good.”
verses.whyNote: Comparison-based observation. This refrain follows the same sequence in both texts, with equivalent ordinal numbers. Its repeated form explains the close correspondence within this chapter; no claim about a liturgical origin or an exceptional rate of agreement across other biblical texts is needed.

words.note: Each day is counted from evening to morning. Israel's days and feasts likewise began at sunset.

readings.saints: God said, “Let there be lights in the firmament of heaven to illuminate the earth and to separate day from night; and let them be for signs and seasons, and for days and years.
readings.hebrew: God said, “Let there be lights in the expanse of the heavens to separate day from night; and let them be for signs and appointed times, and for days and years.
readings.latin: God said, “Let there be lights in the firmament of heaven, and let them separate day from night. Let them serve as signs and mark seasons, days, and years,
readings.kjv: And God said, Let there be lights in the firmament of the heaven to divide the day from the night; and let them be for signs, and for seasons, and for days, and years:

verses.received: God commands lights in the firmament to separate day from night and to serve for signs, seasons, days and years.
verses.explain: The lights are given jobs. They divide day from night and mark out time for those who will live under them. They are placed by God's command, which presents them as servants of his order and not as powers to fear or worship.
shared: God commanded lights in the firmament.
They serve for signs, seasons, days and years.

instructions.text: God gave the lights to separate day from night and to serve for signs, seasons, days and years.
Use the lights to mark time, and give them no worship or fear.

lost.text: Hebrew moadim is the word Leviticus uses for the Lord’s appointed feasts. Greek καιρούς, Latin tempora and King James “seasons” can sound like calendar time. Greek Leviticus 23:4 uses the same word for the feasts, so the link is weakened, not removed.
εἰς φαῦσιν τῆς γῆς states at once that the lights are for illuminating the earth. The other three hold that purpose until 1:15.
φωστῆρες is the word Paul uses for believers shining in a dark world (Philippians 2:15). The Greek reader can hear that connection directly.

flags: Swete’s text has καὶ ἄρχειν τῆς ἡμέρας καὶ τῆς νυκτός, “and to rule the day and the night.” Saints English does not translate it, so the two Greek texts need comparing here.
verses.siteNote: Hebrew me’orot, “lights/luminaries,” corresponds to Greek phōstēres. Greek additionally specifies eis phausin tēs gēs, “to illuminate the earth,” in the opening command. Hebrew mo’adim and Greek kairoi can describe appointed times. Translating Greek as “seasons” here does not exclude sacred occasions: Greek Leviticus 23:4 uses kairoi for the appointed times of the festivals.
verses.whyNote: Pattern-supported hypothesis. The Greek illumination clause matches a purpose also expressed in 1:15 and 1:17, making alignment with those verses plausible. Whether that fuller wording originated in Greek or in a Hebrew source is unresolved. The correspondence of mo’adim and kairoi does not itself establish a loss of festival meaning; compare Leviticus 23:4.

words.note: Sun and moon are not named, only called lights. Paul uses the same Greek word for believers shining in a dark world.
The Hebrew mo'adim is the word Leviticus uses for the appointed feasts of the Lord. From the start, the lights mark times for worship.

readings.saints: Let them give light in the firmament of heaven, so as to shine upon the earth.” And it was so.
readings.hebrew: Let them be lights in the expanse of the heavens to shine upon the earth.” And it was so.
readings.latin: shining in the firmament of heaven and giving light to the earth.” And so it was.
readings.kjv: And let them be for lights in the firmament of the heaven to give light upon the earth: and it was so.

verses.received: The lights are to shine on the earth, and it happens.
verses.explain: The purpose of the lights is stated simply: they exist to give light to the earth. They are there for the sake of the world God is preparing. As before, what he commands comes to pass.
shared: The lights are in the firmament.
They give light upon the earth.

instructions.text: The lights exist to give light upon the earth.

lost.text: The Hebrew plays on one root for light, using it as both noun and verb. The Greek uses two different words. The function of the lights stays the same.

verses.siteNote: Hebrew ve-hayu li-m’orot … le-ha’ir, “let them be for lights … to give light,” uses a noun and then an infinitive from the same root or, “light.” Greek estōsan eis phausin … hōste phainein uses “illumination” and phainein, which here means to shine, not merely to appear.
verses.whyNote: Translation-based hypothesis. Greek recasts Hebrew “for lights … to give light” as “for illumination … so as to shine.” These are different constructions for the same function. The following fulfillment formula agrees, so no separate event is introduced.

words.note: Daniel promises that the wise will shine like the brightness of the firmament, using the same Greek word.

readings.saints: God made the two great lights: the greater light to rule the day, and the lesser light to rule the night, and the stars.
readings.hebrew: God made the two great lights: the greater light to rule the day, and the lesser light to rule the night, and the stars.
readings.latin: God made two great lights: the greater light to rule the day, and the lesser light to rule the night, and the stars.
readings.kjv: And God made two great lights; the greater light to rule the day, and the lesser light to rule the night: he made the stars also.

verses.received: God makes the two great lights, the greater to rule the day and the lesser to rule the night, and the stars.
verses.explain: All four translations call them only the greater and lesser lights, without naming the sun or moon. The bright things in the sky are shown as made by God and given their tasks. Even the stars, so vast to us, are mentioned briefly as his work.

instructions.text: God made the greater light, the lesser light and the stars.
Nothing in the sky rivals God, because all of it is his work.

lost.text: All four hold back the names sun and moon, saying only the greater and lesser lights.
εἰς ἀρχάς uses a word that can mean rule or beginning. Here it means rule, and the site’s note warns against reading “beginnings of the day.”

verses.siteNote: Neither text names the sun or moon; both say “the greater light” and “the lesser light.” Hebrew le-memshelet ha-yom, “to rule the day,” becomes Greek eis archas tēs hēmeras; the Greek term archē has the sense of rule in this context, and “beginnings of the day” would misrepresent its function here.
verses.whyNote: Translation-based observation. The translator kept the descriptive titles instead of substituting the ordinary Greek names hēlios and selēnē, so both texts share the same restraint. The plural archai is a Greek way of expressing dominion and does not change the sense.

words.note: Greek archē means both rule and beginning. The sun and moon are given charge of day and night, which the Psalms praise God for.
The stars are mentioned almost in passing here. Later God shows them to Abram as the measure of his promised offspring.

readings.saints: God set them in the firmament of heaven to shine upon the earth,
readings.hebrew: God set them in the expanse of the heavens to shine upon the earth,
readings.latin: He placed them in the firmament of heaven to shine upon the earth,
readings.kjv: And God set them in the firmament of the heaven to give light upon the earth,

verses.received: God sets the lights in the firmament to shine on the earth.
verses.explain: The lights did not place themselves. God puts them where they belong and gives them their work. Their position in the sky is an act of his care for the earth below.
shared: God put the lights in the firmament.

instructions.text: God himself set the lights in their place to shine upon the earth.

lost.text: Hebrew natan literally says God “gave” them, a verb that can also mean appoint. Greek ἔθετο, Latin posuit and King James “set” keep only the placing.

verses.siteNote: Hebrew va-yitten otam literally says God “gave” them, the verb natan often meaning “set” or “appoint”; Greek etheto, “placed,” chooses the spatial sense. The spatial terms remain distinct: raqia ha-shamayim, “expanse of the heavens,” and stereōma tou ouranou, “firmament of heaven.”
verses.whyNote: Translation-based hypothesis. Hebrew natan covers giving, setting and appointing; the translator selected the Greek verb that fits placement in the sky. The expanse/firmament contrast carries over from 1:6.

words.note: The same Greek verb is used when God sets His bow in the cloud after the flood.

readings.saints: to rule over the day and over the night, and to separate the light from the darkness. God saw that it was good.
readings.hebrew: to rule over the day and over the night, and to separate the light from the darkness. God saw that it was good.
readings.latin: to rule the day and night, and to separate light from darkness. God saw that it was good.
readings.kjv: And to rule over the day and over the night, and to divide the light from the darkness: and God saw that it was good.

verses.received: The lights rule the day and night and separate light from darkness, and God sees that it is good.
verses.explain: The separation God made on the first day is now handed to the lights he has made. Their rule is real, but it is given to them by him. Once again, God looks and calls the work good.
shared: The lights rule day and night.
God saw that it was good.

instructions.text: The rule of the lights over day and night was given to them, and God saw that it was good.
Rule given by God exists to serve the order he made.

lost.text: Nothing here changes the message. The verse repeats the language of 1:4 and hands that separating work to the lights.

verses.siteNote: Hebrew li-mshol ba-yom u-va-laylah, “to rule over the day and over the night,” corresponds to Greek archein tēs hēmeras kai tēs nyktos. The separation of light from darkness repeats the language of 1:4, now assigned to the luminaries, and both texts close with the approval formula.
verses.whyNote: Translation-based observation. The verse reuses vocabulary already fixed earlier in the chapter, and the translator reused his earlier equivalents, so the two readings coincide.

words.note: Light is divided from darkness, not mixed with it. John takes up the pair: the light shines in the darkness, and God is light with no darkness at all.

readings.saints: There was evening and there was morning: a fourth day.
readings.hebrew: There was evening and there was morning: a fourth day.
readings.latin: Evening came, and morning came: the fourth day.
readings.kjv: And the evening and the morning were the fourth day.

verses.received: Evening and morning complete the fourth day.
verses.explain: The refrain closes the day on which the lights were made. The days now have their markers in the sky, and the account continues in the same steady order. Time itself is under God's direction.

instructions.text: God's work continues in an ordered sequence of days.

lost.text: Nothing here changes the message. This is the same refrain as 1:5, 1:8 and 1:13.

verses.siteNote: Hebrew yom revi’i and Greek hēmera tetartē, “a fourth day,” close the day with the same refrain as 1:5, 1:8 and 1:13.
verses.whyNote: Translation-based observation. The fixed refrain is rendered identically, as elsewhere in the chapter.

words.note: Sun, moon and stars come after the plants. Theophilus of Antioch noted that this keeps anyone from treating the stars as the cause of growth.

readings.saints: God said, “Let the waters bring forth creeping things with living souls, and birds flying above the earth along the firmament of heaven.” And it was so.
readings.hebrew: God said, “Let the waters swarm with living creatures, and let birds fly above the earth across the face of the expanse of the heavens.”
readings.latin: God also said, “Let the waters bring forth swarming living creatures, and winged creatures above the earth beneath the firmament of heaven.”
readings.kjv: And God said, Let the waters bring forth abundantly the moving creature that hath life, and fowl that may fly above the earth in the open firmament of heaven.

verses.received: God commands living creatures in the waters and birds above the earth.
verses.explain: The spaces God prepared are now filled. The waters he gathered are to hold living creatures, and the sky he made is to have birds. For the first time the chapter speaks of creatures that move and live, and they come at his command.
shared: The waters are to hold living creatures.
Birds are to be above the earth.

instructions.text: The living creatures of the waters and the birds of the sky came at God's command.

lost.text: The Hebrew has two verbs: the waters swarm, and the birds fly. Greek ἐξαγαγέτω and Latin producant place both under one “bring forth.” The site’s note warns against building a theory of origins on this difference of syntax.
ψυχῶν ζωσῶν speaks of living souls, as do Hebrew nefesh and Latin animæ. The King James “that hath life” drops the word soul.
Only the Greek closes with “and it was so,” matching the pattern of the other commands.

verses.siteNote: Hebrew יִשְׁרְצוּ means “let them swarm,” and its following bird clause uses another verb, yeʿofef, for flying. Greek ἐξαγαγέτω, “let … bring forth,” introduces the waters’ production of living creatures and flying creatures together; it also adds a fulfillment formula. The contrast lies in syntax and presentation. It should not be inflated into a complete theory of biological origins.
verses.whyNote: Proposed explanation; origin unresolved. The leading working explanation is a different construction of the coordinated clauses. The Greek gathers aquatic and flying creatures under a single command to bring forth, giving their emergence a unified presentation. Its added fulfillment formula also fits the repeated command-and-fulfillment pattern of the chapter. This could reflect interpretive translation or a fuller Hebrew source; the comparison alone cannot decide between them. The rabbinic discussion cited above makes it especially unwise to explain the difference as an intentional rejection of Jewish teaching.

readings.saints: God made the great sea creatures and every living soul of moving creatures that the waters brought forth according to their kinds, and every winged bird according to kind. God saw that they were good.
readings.hebrew: God created the great sea creatures and every living creature that moves, with which the waters swarmed according to their kinds, and every winged bird according to its kind. God saw that it was good.
readings.latin: God created the great sea creatures and every living, moving creature that the waters brought forth according to their kinds, and every winged creature according to its kind. God saw that it was good.
readings.kjv: And God created great whales, and every living creature that moveth, which the waters brought forth abundantly, after their kind, and every winged fowl after his kind: and God saw that it was good.

verses.received: God makes the great sea creatures and every kind of living thing in the waters and sky, and sees that this is good.
verses.explain: Even the greatest creatures in the sea are God's work. Nothing in the deep lies outside what he has made, and the creatures of water and air come according to their kinds. God looks over this abundance and approves it.
shared: God made the great sea creatures.
He made the living things of the waters.
God saw that it was good.

instructions.text: God made even the greatest creatures of the sea, and he saw that this was good.
Nothing in the deep needs to be feared as a rival to God.

lost.text: This is the second use of Hebrew bara, and the Greek again has plain ἐποίησεν. Latin creavit and King James “created” keep the distinction.
The Greek says “they were good,” judging the creatures as many. The Hebrew, Latin and King James say “it was good.”
The King James “great whales” narrows the word. Greek κήτη and Latin cete mean huge sea creatures, the term Matthew 12:40 uses for Jonah’s, and Hebrew tanninim elsewhere names sea monsters.

verses.siteNote: This is the second use of bara, “created,” in the chapter; the Greek again has epoiēsen, “made.” Hebrew ha-tanninim ha-gedolim, “the great sea creatures,” becomes ta kētē ta megala. Hebrew sharatsu, “swarmed,” becomes exēgagen, “brought forth,” and the Hebrew approval ki tov, “that it was good,” becomes plural hoti kala, “that they were good.”
verses.whyNote: Translation-based hypothesis. “Made” follows the chapter’s recurring rendering of bara. “Brought forth” corresponds to the Greek command in 1:20. Plural “good” presents the creatures as plural objects of evaluation; Greek can also use singular kalon as a general verdict elsewhere. Thus the plural is not grammatically inevitable, but neither does it express a stronger judgment.

words.greek: kētē ta megala (κήτη τὰ μεγάλα); Hebrew tanninim
words.note: Greek kētos is the word Matthew uses for the creature that swallowed Jonah. The Hebrew tanninim elsewhere names sea monsters.

readings.saints: God blessed them, saying, “Increase and multiply, and fill the waters in the seas; and let the birds multiply upon the earth.”
readings.hebrew: God blessed them, saying, “Be fruitful and multiply, and fill the waters in the seas; and let the birds multiply upon the earth.”
readings.latin: He blessed them, saying, “Increase and multiply, and fill the waters of the sea; and let birds multiply upon the earth.”
readings.kjv: And God blessed them, saying, Be fruitful, and multiply, and fill the waters in the seas, and let fowl multiply in the earth.

verses.received: God blesses the creatures of water and sky and tells them to multiply and fill their realms.
verses.explain: This is the first blessing in the Bible, and it is spoken over fish and birds. God wants the world full of life, not merely filled once. His blessing gives them both the call and the ability to increase.
shared: They are to fill the waters.
Birds are to multiply on the earth.

instructions.text: God blesses living creatures and wants them to increase.
Value animal life as something God has blessed.

lost.text: Hebrew peru contains the word for fruit. Greek αὐξάνεσθε and Latin crescite mean “grow,” so the image is lost. The King James “be fruitful” keeps it.
The Greek word for blessing means to speak a good word over someone, which gives this first blessing in Scripture a spoken sense.

verses.siteNote: Hebrew peru u-revu, “be fruitful and multiply,” pairs a word from peri, “fruit,” with a word for increase. Greek auxanesthe kai plēthynesthe, “grow and multiply,” loses the fruit image but keeps the doubled blessing of abundance. This is the first blessing spoken in the Bible.
verses.whyNote: Translation-based hypothesis. Greek chooses the general growth verb auxanō rather than retaining the Hebrew fruit metaphor directly. Greek does possess a verb for bearing fruit, karpophoreō; Colossians 1:6, 10 even uses it alongside growth language. The difference here is a lexical choice, not a limitation of the Greek language. The same blessing vocabulary recurs in Genesis 1:28.

words.note: The first blessing in Scripture is spoken over fish and birds, and it is a blessing of fruitfulness. Greek eulogeō means to speak a good word.

readings.saints: There was evening and there was morning: a fifth day.
readings.hebrew: There was evening and there was morning: a fifth day.
readings.latin: Evening came, and morning came: the fifth day.
readings.kjv: And the evening and the morning were the fifth day.

verses.received: Evening and morning complete the fifth day.
verses.explain: The refrain closes the day of the sea creatures and birds. Water and sky are now full of life. The steady rhythm carries the account toward the land animals and humanity.

instructions.text: God's work continues in an ordered sequence of days.

lost.text: Nothing here changes the message. This is the same refrain as 1:5, 1:8, 1:13 and 1:19.

verses.siteNote: Hebrew yom chamishi and Greek hēmera pemptē, “a fifth day,” close the day with the standard refrain.
verses.whyNote: Translation-based observation. The fixed refrain is rendered identically, as elsewhere in the chapter.

words.note: The six days form two sets of three: the first three shape spaces (light, sky and sea, land) and the next three fill them (lights, birds and fish, animals and man).

readings.saints: God said, “Let the earth bring forth living creatures according to kind: four-footed animals, creeping things, and wild animals of the earth according to kind.” And it was so.
readings.hebrew: God said, “Let the earth bring forth living creatures according to their kinds: livestock, creeping things, and wild animals of the earth according to their kinds.” And it was so.
readings.latin: God also said, “Let the earth bring forth living creatures according to their kinds: livestock, creeping creatures, and wild animals of the earth according to their kinds.” And so it was.
readings.kjv: And God said, Let the earth bring forth the living creature after his kind, cattle, and creeping thing, and beast of the earth after his kind: and it was so.

verses.received: God commands the earth to bring forth living creatures, including wild animals and creeping things, each according to its kind.
verses.explain: The land receives its creatures as the sea and sky received theirs. God speaks, and the earth is to bring them forth in their kinds. The world is being filled in an orderly way, and what he says happens.
shared: It is to bring forth living creatures.
They come according to their kinds.

instructions.text: The land animals came at God's command, each according to its kind.

lost.text: τετράποδα, “four-footed animals,” is a broader class than Hebrew behemah, Latin jumenta or King James “cattle.” Peter’s vision in Acts 10:12 uses the same Greek word.
The Greek does not hold one word for the domestic animals. It has τετράποδα here and κτήνη in 1:25, so the plain repeat of Hebrew behemah across the two verses disappears.

verses.siteNote: Hebrew behemah, “livestock” or domestic animals, becomes Greek tetrapoda, “four-footed animals,” a broader descriptive class; in 1:25 the Greek uses a different word, ktēnē, for livestock. Hebrew nefesh chayah, “living creature” (literally “living soul”), becomes psychēn zōsan, and remes, “creeping things,” becomes herpeta.
verses.whyNote: Translation-based hypothesis. The adjacent verses demonstrate that Greek can render Hebrew behemah with either tetrapoda (four-footed animals) or ktēnē (livestock). Lexical variation can explain the contrast without positing a different Hebrew noun. The translator’s precise stylistic or interpretive motive is not recoverable from this pair alone.

words.note: Peter sees four-footed creatures, creeping things and birds let down in a sheet, the same list as creation, when he learns that God shows no partiality.

readings.saints: God made the wild animals of the earth according to kind, and the livestock according to kind, and all the creeping things of the earth according to their kinds. God saw that they were good.
readings.hebrew: God made the wild animals of the earth according to their kinds, and the livestock according to their kinds, and every creeping thing of the ground according to its kind. God saw that it was good.
readings.latin: God made the wild animals of the earth according to their kinds, the livestock, and every creeping creature of the earth according to its kind. God saw that it was good,
readings.kjv: And God made the beast of the earth after his kind, and cattle after their kind, and every thing that creepeth upon the earth after his kind: and God saw that it was good.

verses.received: God makes the wild animals, the livestock and the creeping things, and sees that this is good.
verses.explain: God himself makes the creatures of the land, large and small, wild and tame. None is an accident or an afterthought. He looks at them all and gives the same approval he has given throughout the chapter.
shared: God saw that it was good.

instructions.text: God made the animals of the land and saw that this was good.
Treat animals as creatures God made and approved.

lost.text: As in 1:21, the Greek says “they were good,” and the Hebrew, Latin and King James say “it was good.”
The Hebrew uses two nouns, erets for earth and adamah for ground. The Greek uses one word, γῆ, so that distinction is lost before the man is formed from the ground in chapter 2.
The Latin ends this verse with a comma and runs straight into 1:26.

verses.siteNote: The creature groups agree. Hebrew remes ha-adamah, “creeping thing of the ground,” uses adamah, the soil from which adam will be formed in 2:7; Greek herpeta tēs gēs, “of the earth,” does not preserve that wordplay. The Greek again uses plural agreement, “they were good.”
verses.whyNote: Translation-based hypothesis. Greek uses gē for both Hebrew erets and adamah in this verse, so the English earth/ground distinction is not reproduced by two Greek nouns. Plural kala, “good,” evaluates the listed creatures as a plurality, as in 1:21; it does not introduce a different level of goodness.

readings.saints: God said, “Let us make humankind according to our image and according to likeness; and let them rule over the fish of the sea, the birds of the sky, the livestock, all the earth, and every creeping thing that creeps upon the earth.”
readings.hebrew: God said, “Let us make humankind in our image, according to our likeness; and let them rule over the fish of the sea, the birds of the sky, the livestock, all the earth, and every creeping thing that creeps upon the earth.”
readings.latin: and said, “Let Us make humankind in Our image and likeness, and let them rule the fish of the sea, the birds of heaven, the animals, the whole earth, and every creeping creature that moves upon the earth.”
readings.kjv: And God said, Let us make man in our image, after our likeness: and let them have dominion over the fish of the sea, and over the fowl of the air, and over the cattle, and over all the earth, and over every creeping thing that creepeth upon the earth.

verses.received: God resolves to make humanity in the divine image and to give humanity rule over the creatures and the earth.
verses.explain: The pattern changes here. In place of a simple command, God says "let us make," and what is made will bear his image. Humanity is given a unique place: made like God and entrusted with care over the living world.
shared: Humanity is made in God's image and likeness.
Humanity is to rule over the fish, birds, animals and earth.

instructions.text: God made humanity in his image and likeness and purposed that they should rule over the creatures and the earth.
Rule over creation as those who bear God's image, reflecting his goodness.

lost.text: Hebrew and King James put “our” on both image and likeness. The Greek attaches ἡμετέραν only to the image and leaves καθ’ ὁμοίωσιν standing alone. The Latin places nostram after the pair, so it can cover both.
εἰκών is the word Paul uses for Christ as the image of the invisible God (Colossians 1:15). The Greek reader can hear that connection directly.
All four keep “let us,” and the grammar alone does not settle who is addressed. The Latin præsit is singular, “let him rule,” while the Greek ἀρχέτωσαν is plural.
ἄνθρωπον means a human being or humanity. The King James “man” can now sound narrower than that.

flags: The Latin–English column prints “let them rule,” but the Clementine Latin has singular præsit.
verses.siteNote: Hebrew na’aseh adam be-tsalmenu ki-dmutenu, “let us make humankind in our image, according to our likeness,” has the possessive “our” on both nouns. Greek kat’ eikona hēmeteran kai kath’ homoiōsin attaches “our” only to image. Hebrew adam is collective, “humankind,” matching the plural “let them rule”; Greek anthrōpos works the same way. The grammar alone does not identify the addressees of “let us.”
verses.whyNote: Translation-based hypothesis. Greek expresses “our” once and adds “and” between image and likeness. A shared possessive sense can be understood across the coordinated phrases; stylistic compression is possible, but its motive is not documented. The omission of a second possessive does not by itself show a theological alteration. Both readings retain the plural deliberation that the commentators interpret differently.

words.note: God speaks in the plural. Early Christian writers read it as the Father speaking with the Son and the Spirit; it is also read as a plural of majesty, or God addressing His heavenly court.
Man is made according to God's image. Paul calls Christ Himself the image of the invisible God.

readings.saints: God made humankind; according to the image of God He made him; male and female He made them.
readings.hebrew: God created humankind in His image; in the image of God He created him; male and female He created them.
readings.latin: God created humankind in His image; in the image of God He created them; male and female He created them.
readings.kjv: So God created man in his own image, in the image of God created he him; male and female created he them.

verses.received: God makes humanity in God's image, male and female.
verses.explain: What God resolved to do, he now does. Every person bears the image of God, and that dignity is given to male and female alike. This is the high point of the chapter's account of what God has made.
shared: He made them in the image of God.
He made them male and female.

instructions.text: Humanity, male and female, is made in the image of God.
Honor every man and woman as bearing the image of God.

lost.text: The Hebrew is a three-line poem with “created” three times and “image” twice. The Greek says “made” three times and has only one image clause, so both the creating word and the doubled line are gone. The Latin and King James keep them.
ἄρσεν καὶ θῆλυ is the phrase behind Jesus’ teaching on marriage in Matthew 19:4 and Mark 10:6, and Paul’s pairing in Galatians 3:28.

flags: The Latin–English column prints “created them” in the second line, but the Clementine Latin has singular illum, “him.”
verses.siteNote: The Hebrew is a three-line poem with bara, “created,” three times and tselem, “image,” twice: “in His image … in the image of God … male and female.” The Greek has epoiēsen, “made,” and lacks the first “in His image,” keeping only kat’ eikona theou. Singular “him” and plural “them” belong to both texts’ collective description of humanity; zakhar u-neqevah is rendered exactly by arsen kai thēly.
verses.whyNote: Origin unresolved. The Greek has a shorter image-clause sequence while retaining three occurrences of “made.” Translational compression or a difference in the Hebrew source are possible explanations. The compared editions do not establish a copying accident, negligence, or a deliberate theological change. Both readings explicitly affirm humanity’s creation in God’s image.

words.note: Jesus quotes these words when He speaks about marriage. Paul uses the same pair when he says that in Christ there is no male and female.

readings.saints: God blessed them, saying, “Increase and multiply, and fill the earth and exercise dominion over it; and rule over the fish of the sea, the birds of the sky, all the livestock, all the earth, and every creeping thing that creeps upon the earth.”
readings.hebrew: God blessed them, and God said to them, “Be fruitful and multiply, and fill the earth and subdue it; and rule over the fish of the sea, the birds of the sky, and every living thing that moves upon the earth.”
readings.latin: God blessed them and said, “Increase and multiply; fill the earth and subdue it. Rule the fish of the sea, the birds of heaven, and every living creature that moves upon the earth.”
readings.kjv: And God blessed them, and God said unto them, Be fruitful, and multiply, and replenish the earth, and subdue it: and have dominion over the fish of the sea, and over the fowl of the air, and over every living thing that moveth upon the earth.

verses.received: God blesses humanity and tells them to multiply, fill the earth and rule over it.
verses.explain: God speaks a blessing over people as he did over the sea creatures and birds, and he speaks directly to them. They are to increase, fill the earth and take responsibility for it. Human work and family life are presented here as part of God's good purpose.
shared: They are to multiply and fill the earth.
They are to rule over the fish, birds and living things.

instructions.text: God tells humanity to multiply, fill the earth and subdue it, and to rule over the fish, the birds and the living things.
God's blessing comes before his command.
Family and responsible work are part of God's good purpose for mankind.

lost.text: The Greek gives the fuller list of what humanity rules, naming livestock, all the earth and creeping things. The Hebrew, Latin and King James have the shorter “every living thing that moves.”
κατακυριεύσατε, “exercise lordship,” is a different picture from Hebrew kivshuha and Latin subjicite, “subdue,” which the King James follows.
As in 1:22, the Greek and Latin “grow” lose the fruit image in Hebrew peru. The King James keeps it.
The King James “replenish” meant “fill” in 1611. A modern reader can wrongly hear “fill again.”

verses.siteNote: Hebrew has “God blessed them, and God said to them”; Greek links the blessing directly to legōn, “saying,” as in 1:22. Hebrew kivshuha, “subdue it,” corresponds to Greek katakyrieusate autēs, “exercise lordship over it.” Greek’s dominion list additionally names livestock and all the earth, and specifies creeping things where Hebrew has every living thing that moves. These are differences in wording and list structure, not extra phrases to be supplied in the Hebrew column.
verses.whyNote: Pattern-supported hypothesis. Greek’s fuller dominion list closely corresponds to its list in 1:26, although “all” with livestock is more explicit in 1:28. The blessing followed by “saying” corresponds to 1:22. These patterns make alignment plausible, but they do not establish whether it occurred in translation or in a Hebrew textual form behind the Greek.

readings.saints: God said, “Behold, I have given you every seed-bearing plant sowing seed upon all the earth, and every tree with seed-bearing fruit within it; they shall be food for you.
readings.hebrew: God said, “Behold, I have given you every plant yielding seed upon the face of all the earth, and every tree with seed-bearing fruit; they shall be food for you.
readings.latin: God said, “See, I have given you every seed-bearing plant upon the earth, and all trees that have within them seed of their own kind, to be your food,
readings.kjv: And God said, Behold, I have given you every herb bearing seed, which is upon the face of all the earth, and every tree, in the which is the fruit of a tree yielding seed; to you it shall be for meat.

verses.received: God gives humanity seed-bearing plants and trees for food.
verses.explain: God does not only give people work; he provides for them. Food comes as his gift, and the seed within it means the provision can continue. The one who made humanity also sustains humanity.
shared: God says "behold," drawing attention to his gift.
He has given the seed-bearing plants.
They are to be food for people.

instructions.text: God assigns seed-bearing plants and trees to humanity for food.
Human food is presented as God's gift.
Receive food with gratitude, as something given.

lost.text: σπόριμον σπεῖρον σπέρμα states the seed idea twice over, tying this gift back to 1:11–12.
The Greek drops the Hebrew idiom “the face of all the earth,” which the King James keeps. The place meant does not change.
The Latin says the trees hold “seed of their own kind,” with no separate word for their fruit.

verses.siteNote: Hebrew hinneh natatti lakhem, “behold, I have given you,” is matched by Greek idou dedōka hymin. Hebrew esev zorea zera … al penei khol ha-arets, “plant yielding seed upon the face of all the earth,” becomes chorton sporimon speiron sperma … epanō pasēs tēs gēs, which states the seed-bearing quality twice and drops “the face of.” Le-okhlah, “for food,” becomes eis brōsin.
verses.whyNote: Translation-based hypothesis. Greek reinforces the seed vocabulary with an adjective and a participle and expresses the location without Hebrew’s “face of” idiom. These choices fit the seed language already used in 1:11–12. They can be understood as translation and emphasis, but their precise motivation is not documented. Both passages grant plants and fruit as food.

words.note: At first plants are given for food. Meat is given after the flood, with the green plants named again as the comparison.

readings.saints: And to all the wild animals of the earth, all the birds of the sky, and every creeping thing that creeps upon the earth, which has within it a soul of life, I give every green plant for food.” And it was so.
readings.hebrew: And to every wild animal of the earth, every bird of the sky, and everything that moves upon the earth in which there is a living soul, I give every green plant for food.” And it was so.
readings.latin: and food for every animal of the earth, every bird of heaven, and everything that moves upon the earth and has living breath.” And so it was.
readings.kjv: And to every beast of the earth, and to every fowl of the air, and to every thing that creepeth upon the earth, wherein there is life, I have given every green herb for meat: and it was so.

verses.received: God provides food for every animal, bird and creeping thing that has life.
verses.explain: God's care reaches beyond humanity to all that lives. Animals, birds and creeping things are provided for, just as people are. Nothing he made is left without what it needs, and again it is so.
shared: God provides for the animals of the earth.
He provides for the creatures that move on the earth.

instructions.text: God provides food for the animals, the birds and the creatures that move on the earth.
God's care extends to all living things, and his people can reflect that care.

lost.text: The Greek, Hebrew and King James name the green plant here. The Latin says only that the creatures may have something to feed on, leaving the reader to supply it from 1:29.
ψυχὴν ζωῆς, “a soul of life,” keeps the word soul, as do Hebrew nefesh and Latin anima. The King James “wherein there is life” does not.

verses.siteNote: Both continue the grant of food; “I give” supplies the verb carried forward from 1:29. Hebrew nefesh chayah, “a living soul,” becomes Greek psychē zōēs, “a soul of life,” and Hebrew romes, “moves,” becomes herpon, “creeps.” Hebrew yereq esev, “green plant,” becomes chorton chlōron.
verses.whyNote: Translation-based hypothesis. Hebrew nefesh chayah combines a noun with the adjective “living”; Greek psychē zōēs uses a genitive, “soul of life.” It is therefore a change of construction, not a literal reproduction of a Hebrew construct chain. Greek also continues its creeping-thing vocabulary. The expressions differ while the provision of green plants agrees.

words.note: Animals also receive plants for food. After the flood, God gives man all things "as the green plants", recalling this verse.

readings.saints: God saw all the things that He had made, and behold, they were very good. There was evening and there was morning: a sixth day.
readings.hebrew: God saw everything that He had made, and behold, it was very good. There was evening and there was morning: the sixth day.
readings.latin: God saw everything He had made, and it was very good. Evening came, and morning came: the sixth day.
readings.kjv: And God saw every thing that he had made, and, behold, it was very good. And the evening and the morning were the sixth day.

verses.received: God sees all that he has made and finds it very good, and the sixth day ends.
verses.explain: God looks over the whole of creation, and the verdict rises from good to very good. The chapter ends with a world that is ordered, full and approved by its maker. This is the setting for everything that follows in the Bible.
shared: God saw everything he had made.

instructions.text: God saw everything he had made, and it was very good.
Value the created world as God values it, and thank him for it.

lost.text: τὰ πάντα and καλὰ λίαν are plural, viewing all things together as very good. The Latin agrees. The Hebrew and King James use a collective “it.”
The Hebrew marks “the sixth day” as the first day in the chapter with the definite article. The Greek and Latin have none, and the King James uses “the” for every day, so the emphasis cannot be seen.
The Latin drops “behold,” which the Greek ἰδού, Hebrew hinneh and King James keep.

verses.siteNote: Hebrew et kol asher asah … tov me’od, “everything that He had made … very good,” is a collective singular; Greek ta panta … kala lian is plural. Hebrew yom ha-shishi, “the sixth day,” is the first day in the chapter to carry the definite article; the Greek hēmera hektē has none. “Very” (me’od) and lian are equivalent in strength.
verses.whyNote: Translation-based hypothesis. Greek presents “all things” and “very good” in the plural and leaves the ordinal without an article, as in the preceding day refrains. This supports a possible preference for a uniform Greek formula but does not document the translator’s purpose. Rashi’s interpretation depends on a Hebrew article that this Greek wording does not reproduce; “very good” has equivalent force in both.

words.note: Only after man is made does the verdict become "very good". Paul writes that everything God created is good.
